activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark.
story:
Noah had been staring at the night sky for twenty minutes and the Moon was nowhere. "It vanished," he told Priya at lunch. "Yesterday it was a big white blob next to the science wing, and today it's just gone. Like somebody erased it."

"Moons don't vanish," Priya said, dunking her fry in ketchup.

"Then explain where it went."

She couldn't, which bothered Noah all afternoon. In science, Mr. Okafor had set up a lamp on a stool and handed out white styrofoam balls, one per table. "Show me why the Moon changes shape," he said, and then he sat at his desk and graded quizzes, offering nothing else.

Noah stuck a pencil through their ball so he could hold it up, and Priya clicked on the lamp. First he made the ball circle the pencil slowly, watching nothing change, which felt like a waste of time. Then he realized he should be moving around it himself, or moving the ball around Priya, who was playing Earth. He held the ball out at arm's length and walked a circle around her chair.

"Stop," Priya said, when the ball was between her and the lamp. "Look at this. From here I can't see any of the lit part at all. The bright side is facing the lamp, which is away from me."

Noah spun the ball so he could see it from his own angle. Half the styrofoam was blindingly white in the lamp light, and the other half was shadow gray. From Priya's spot, only the gray showed. "So the Moon's still there," he said slowly. "At new moon it's roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark."

"That's why you couldn't find it," Priya said. "It didn't vanish. It was showing us its back."

Noah kept orbiting her chair, stopping at each quarter turn so she could call out the shape she saw: a sliver, a half, a fat oval, then nothing again. He felt like he'd found the hidden gear inside a machine. He wrote his last night's sky in his notebook and drew a line through "vanished," writing instead "anomaly solved." Mr. Okafor wandered by, watched one full orbit, and said, "Nice. You two should illustrate that for the class on Friday."

"But what if we mess up in front of everyone?" Priya asked.

"Then we mess up and try it again," Noah said. "The Moon gets three chances a month. We get at least one."

He walked another slow circle, ball held high, and Priya tracked it with her eyes until it slipped once more into the dark.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Fractions can only be added directly when their denominators match, because the denominator names the size of the pieces being counted.
story:
Alexandra spread her fraction cards across the table in the math club room and frowned at them. Her problem was simple and urgent: the club's bake sale was Saturday, and she had promised to bring exactly one cup of granola, but her grandmother's recipe called for a half cup of oats and a third cup of seeds, and she could not figure out whether that made a whole cup or not. Half plus third. She wrote "1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5" on her paper, because two and five were the numbers she had.

Across the table, Marcus was stacking his cards into a tower, which was what he did when he wanted to look busy without actually solving anything. He had a reputation for finishing worksheets first, but today he kept glancing at Alexandra's paper. "That's wrong," he said finally. "It has to be more than a half, and two fifths is less than a half."

Alexandra looked at her answer. He was right, and she had not even noticed. She flipped her cards over so the shaded pie drawings faced up: a circle cut in two, a circle cut in three. "You can't count these together," she said slowly. "The pieces aren't the same size." Last summer at her grandmother's house she had learned the same thing with real measuring cups, pouring a half cup of flour and then a third cup and watching the bowl, because her grandmother's old cups had no markings and she had to guess whether she'd reached one cup. She had guessed wrong that day, and the cookies had spread flat as pancakes.

She pulled out a fresh card and drew a rectangle, then divided it into six thin columns, darkening three of them, then two more. Sixths. Both the half and the third could live on the same rectangle. Three sixths plus two sixths made five sixths. "The denominator names the size of the pieces," she said, mostly to herself, and Marcus leaned over so far his card tower toppled.

"Wait, do it again with fourths and eighths," he said, grabbing a pencil, because if she had found a trick that worked, he wanted to be the one who used it fastest. Alexandra drew another rectangle and slid the pencil across the table to him.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
story:
Sara's grandmother had a habit that made no sense to her: twice a month, she refused rice. Not once, not on random Tuesdays, but twice, and never when Sara expected it. One night Grandma would pass the rice pot to Sara's dad and eat only fruit and milk, laughing while everyone else had seconds. "Are you on some secret diet?" Sara asked once. Grandma only smiled and said her stomach was resting, like a student on a school holiday.

So Sara turned detective. She dismantled the kitchen calendar from its hook and carried it to her room, where she circled every day Grandma had skipped rice, according to her mom's memory and her own notes from the last two months. The circles didn't land on weekdays, which would have been too easy. They didn't land on the same dates either. Six circles sat there like footprints with no trail, and Sara glared at them while chewing her pencil.

Then Mom mentioned, almost by accident, that the family followed the moon's calendar for festivals, not the square one on the wall. Sara looked up the lunar month and found it split in two halves. She counted forward from the new moon and the full moon, and both times her pencil landed on the same number. Eleven. Every single circle. She counted twice more, because she didn't trust herself, and then she ran downstairs yelling, "It's the eleventh day! Both halves! Mom, it's the eleventh day every time!"

Mom laughed so hard she had to sit down. "That day is called Ekadashi," she said. "Your grandmother keeps it for Vishnu. No grains, no beans."

"Grains and beans," Sara repeated, writing it on her hand so she wouldn't forget. Then she made a decision, quickly, because Grandma was coming to visit tomorrow and Sara wanted to surprise her. She would keep the day too, at least until dinner.

The next morning Sara hid the toaster from herself, which mostly meant putting a chair in front of it. By lunch she was hungry enough to consider eating the chair. Her little brother, home with a cold and a spoonful of antibiotic, offered her his crackers out of pure mischief. "Those are grains," she said grandly, and pushed them back.

When Grandma arrived, Sara set the table with fruit and milk at her own place and waited. Grandma looked at the plate, then at Sara, and raised one eyebrow. "Eleventh day," Sara said. "Ekadashi. Grains and beans, gone."

Grandma sat down slowly and pressed her hand over her heart. "You counted?"

"I counted."

Then Grandma picked up a banana, sliced it in half, and set the bigger piece on Sara's plate.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many shelf labels show a unit price, such as the price per litre, so different sizes can be compared; the bigger carton is often, but not always, cheaper per litre.
story:
Mya folded her third towel and checked the window again. Her mother had left one armload of laundry and a five-dollar bill on the folding table, then pointed down the street toward Pansik's corner store. "We need two litres of milk," she'd said. "You can handle it." Mya had said "sure" in a voice that came out more hesitant than she meant it to, and now her mother was gone and the dryers were humming and it was just her, the towels, and the five dollars.

The store was two blocks away. Mya knew the route; she had walked it a hundred times, but always with somebody. Alone, the sidewalk felt longer, like it had been secretly stretched while nobody was watching. She decided not to think about that, because thinking about it would use up all her stamina before she even got to the dairy case. She counted cracks in the pavement instead, and by the time she counted forty-one, she was pushing open the door of Pansik's with the little bell jingling above her head.

The milk shelf held two options. One big two-litre carton for $3.49, or small one-litre cartons for $1.85 each. Two small ones would make two litres too. She reached for the big carton first, because big things always seemed like the deal, but then her eye caught the tiny print on the shelf label. Under the big price it said "unit price" and then a number, and the small cartons' label had one too. She looked back and forth. "It's the price per litre," said the man behind the counter, watching her. "So you can compare sizes." Mya frowned, did the math, and winced. Two small cartons came to $3.70, more than the big one. But then she checked the shelf one row down, where the chocolate milk sat, and there the bigger bottle had a higher price per litre than the small one. So it wasn't a rule. It was just a thing you had to check.

She put the big carton on the counter and handed over the five. The clerk gave her back a toonie and two quarters and a penny, and she counted it right there in front of him, slowly, tapping each coin on the counter. Six dollars and one cent would have been wrong. A dollar fifty-one was right. "First time?" he asked. "First time alone," she said, and he nodded like that was the more important version anyway.

Walking back, she thought about last summer, when she'd refused to go to the store even with her cousin, because a dog on Miller Street had once barked at her and she'd decided the whole street was off-limits. That had cost her a whole summer of Freezies. She still wasn't sure the dog had been harmless. But she was sure about the milk.

At the laundromat, her mother was pulling warm towels from the dryer. Mya set the carton on the folding table and lined up the coins in a neat row. "Fifty-one cents," she said. "And next time, I'm checking the unit price before I grab anything."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: An oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius.
story:
The zucchini on the table gleamed like little green submarines, and Alexis intended to turn three of them into muffins before lunch. Her grandmother had emailed the recipe from Arizona, and the first line said: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Alexis's family's oven, however, had been bought in Lisbon, and its dial only went by Celsius, which was like being handed directions in a language she'd studied for exactly one week.

"What does 350 even mean?" her little brother Theo asked, peering over her shoulder at the phone. "Three hundred fifty what? Dragons?"

"Degrees, obviously." But obvious it was not. The dial climbed from 100 to 250, and nowhere did it say 350, so somewhere between the recipe and the oven, the numbers had to be hiding a rule. Last summer, Alexis remembered, she had tried to bake cookies at the highest number on the dial because it seemed logical that hotter meant faster. The cookies had come out like charcoal coasters, and her grandmother had laughed so hard she'd had to sit down. Alexis did not want a repeat of the Great Charcoal Incident.

She set the zucchini on the cutting board and tried to classify the problem in her head. Same recipe, different numbers, so the two systems had to be measuring the same heat with different names, like a cat named Gato. The question was the ratio, and ratios could be hunted. "We're going to the farmers' market," she announced. "The bread stall. Bakers know ovens."

At the market, Mrs. Almeida was arranging loaves in diagonal rows across her table, tilting each one so the slashes in the crust caught the morning light. Alexis explained her dilemma, holding up the phone like evidence in a trial.

"Ah, the American recipes," Mrs. Almeida said, wiping flour off her hands. "Three hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit is about one hundred seventy-five to one hundred eighty Celsius. My daughter-in-law bakes from those websites all the time."

Alexis did the arithmetic twice, because a wrong oven setting was how monarchies fell, and she was not going to lose her muffin empire the same way. She dialled to 175 and waited while the oven ticked and hummed its way up to temperature. She grated the zucchini, cracked the eggs, and folded the batter with the patience of someone who had once produced charcoal and learned from it.

The muffins rose into golden domes, and Theo grabbed one before it had even left the pan. "Ow. Ow. Worth it," he said around a mouthful, and Alexis slid the rest onto a cooling rack, diagonal like Mrs. Almeida's loaves, because presentation mattered.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
story:
"Two minutes?" Harrison said, bouncing a tennis ball off the garage wall. "You can't say anything important in two minutes."

His sister Maya looked up from her phone. "Mr. Reyes assigned you a two-minute speech. That's the assignment. Opening hook, three points, closing."

"Two minutes is nothing. That's like the time it takes to microwave a burrito."

Maya grinned, which meant she knew something he didn't. "The Gettysburg Address. Abraham Lincoln, November 19, 1863. It was about 272 words long, and it took roughly two minutes to deliver. That speech is famous, and it was shorter than your book report."

Harrison caught the ball and stared at her. Two minutes. Two hundred seventy-two words. That meant the rule wasn't "say less," it was "say only what counts." Every extra word would exclude a better one, the way his mom removed junk from the garage to make room for the ping-pong table. If Lincoln could do it, so could he.

He grabbed his notebook and wrote fast. Hook: a question about why nobody remembers the two-hour speech that came before Lincoln's. Three points, each one sentence. Closing: the burrito line, because if his classmates were going to remember anything, it would be that.

"You're actually excited," Maya said. "Weird."

"It's like a puzzle. I get exactly 272 words and I have to make every single one matter."

He rehearsed in the kitchen while she timed him. First run: two minutes forty. He cut words until his throat hurt. Second run: one minute fifty-five. Close enough. He added back "roughly," just to be exact.

The morning of the speech, Harrison stood in front of the class with his palms sweating and his heart hammering, and watched heads actually lift when he opened with the question about the forgotten two-hour speaker.

After class, Mr. Reyes stopped him at the door. "Where did you learn that about Lincoln?"

"My sister. She's kind of infectious that way." Harrison grinned. "Ask her about the income tax speech she has to give next week. It's three minutes, and she's furious about the extra one."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: In the gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford, most alpha particles passed straight through, showing an atom is mostly empty space.
story:
Parker stood in the Build-an-Atom room of the science museum, holding a tray of marbles, pompoms, and Styrofoam balls, and glaring at the instruction card like it had insulted his sneakers. The card said: construct a model of an atom with protons, neutrons, and electrons in the right places. Right places? Nobody had ever shown him an atom. They were sneaky like that.

He started cramming. Red marbles for protons, gray marbles for neutrons, all smooshed into a fat Styrofoam ball, with blue pompoms stuck on the outside like sprinkles. It looked like a donut that had given up on life. Beside him, a girl named Ruby was doing the exact same thing, packing her foam ball solid with beads and humming, completely confident.

"You're making yours solid too?" Parker asked.

"Obviously," Ruby said. "Stuff is stuff. Solid stuff is solid."

Something itched in Parker's brain. He flashed back to last summer, when his grandfather had taken him to this same museum and they'd stood in front of a big display with a glowing gold sheet in the middle. His grandfather had read the plaque out loud, slowly, the way he read everything. The gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford. They fired alpha particles at gold foil, and most of the alpha particles passed straight through. The plaque's last line had said it plainly: an atom is mostly empty space.

Mostly empty. Parker looked at his jam-packed foam ball and felt his ears go warm. If atoms were mostly empty space, then his model was like drawing a crowded swimming pool to represent a desert.

"Wait," he said. "We're doing it wrong. Rutherford proved atoms are mostly empty space. Geiger and Marsden shot alpha particles at gold foil, and most of them passed straight through."

Ruby squinted at him, clearly deciding whether he was biased in favor of his own cleverness. "Passed through gold? Gold is metal. Metal stops my teeth."

"The experiment says it, not me," Parker said. He pulled the marbles back out of his ball, which made a sad, squeaky sound, and clumped the protons and neutrons into one tight knot in the center. Then he hung electrons far out on wire loops, alone in all that nothing. The model suddenly looked like a tiny solar system floating in a lot of lonely dark.

Ruby poked a finger through the empty space around her own bead ball. "Huh," she said. "My hand is basically not touching anything. Somewhere in there. Sort of."

A museum volunteer strolled by, announced that the model jury would vote on favorite atoms at three o'clock, and warned that she would strictly enforce the no-gluing-your-fingers rule, since last week had been a disaster. Parker and Ruby looked at each other.

"Want to fuse our leftover beads into a giant electron?" Parker asked, holding up the shiniest one.

Ruby grabbed the wire. "Only if I get to make it wobble."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real feeding relationships form a food web of many linked chains rather than one single chain.
story:
Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table and weighed the corners with four smooth stones from the garden path. Her assignment was due Monday: draw a food chain, starting with the sun, ending with a top predator, and explain what would happen if one link disappeared. She had chosen the pond in her own backyard because she could watch it instead of guessing.

She began with what she could see. Sunlight fed the algae and the pondweed, so she drew the sun with long yellow rays touching a green smear of plants. Then came the snails, rasping quietly on the stones at the edge. Then the mallard duck that paddled across the water every afternoon, and at the top, the fox she had spotted once at dusk, slipping along the fence line. Sun, plants, snails, duck, fox. She wrote the arrows carefully and sat back, pleased with how neat it looked.

Her little brother Theo came out with a cup of crackers and leaned over her shoulder. "Why's the duck eating snails?" he asked. "I saw him munching the weeds this morning. Right over there." Elena started to say he was wrong, then stopped. She had seen that too, hadn't she? The duck tipping forward, tail in the air, tearing at the pondweed. She got her binoculars from the porch and settled onto the grass to watch. For twenty minutes she kept her eyes on the water. The duck ate pondweed. Then it gulped something small from a rock, and when Elena checked the spot, the rock was empty of the snail that had been there before.

"So he eats both," she said slowly. Her beautiful chain had a duck with two arrows coming in, from plants and from snails. And the snails, she realized, ate the algae, which was different from the pondweed. That meant there wasn't just one chain. There were chains that crossed. She grabbed a fresh board and started again, letting arrows branch and tangle until the whole page looked like a net. "It's a food web," she told Theo, holding it up. "Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so the chains get linked together." Theo nodded, mouth full, and pointed at the fox. "What about him?"

Elena thought about her teacher's question, the one about losing a link. She covered the snail with her thumb. The duck still had the plants, so the duck would be fine, and so would the fox. But cover the plants instead and the snails would go hungry too, because they needed the algae, and then the duck would lose both meals at once. One missing thing could shake several chains. She drew a big red X experimentally across the plants, then wiped it away.

"Why do you keep erasing and drawing it again?" Theo asked, shivering a little in the shade. Elena draped the old blanket from the porch swing around his shoulders and handed him the last of her crackers, since he'd finished his. "Because my motivation was to make it neat," she said, "but the pond isn't neat. The pond is messy and connected, and I kind of cherish that now." Theo chewed, watching the duck glide past the reeds, and Elena bent back over her tangled, crossing, truthful arrows.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: The prime meridian, at 0 degrees longitude, was set through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, by an international conference held in Washington, D.C., in 1884.
story:
The wall map in Delgado Travel was bigger than the one at school, and Oliver stood in front of it with his notebook open and his pencil going nowhere. His teacher had asked for the exact location of one city, given in latitude and longitude, and Oliver had picked London mostly because it sounded easy. Now he was staring at the thin curved lines covering the ocean like a net, and he could not figure out where zero was supposed to start.

"Looking for something specific, or just hiding from your mom?" asked Mrs. Delgado, coming out from behind her desk with a stack of brochures. She was small and quick, and today she kept glancing at a poster of the Thames that had been hanging crooked for a month. Her boss had promised that whoever sold the most London packages this spring would get the window display, and Mrs. Delgado wanted that window badly.

"I need London's coordinates," Oliver said. "But I don't get longitude. Latitude goes up and down from the equator, that part's fine. Longitude goes sideways, but sideways from where?" He tapped the map. "There's no middle ocean line to count from. It's like the equator just vanished."

Mrs. Delgado set down her brochures. "Tell you what. Help me fix this poster and straighten the globe stand, and you can use the big magnifier from the desk drawer. Half my customers my age complain the numbers are too small." The globe was old and a little frail, its stand cracked, and when Oliver steadied it with one hand while she tightened a screw, he noticed the zero line of longitude ran right through a notch in England, just past a city called Greenwich. He had assumed the zero line would pass through Washington, D.C., because that was where the big international conference of 1884 had met to settle it. He had read that on a homework sheet and built his whole notebook page around counting east and west from Washington. Clearly that idea was wrong, and he had just tested it against the actual globe.

"So the conference was in Washington," he said slowly, following the line with his finger, "but the zero isn't. It's here, at Greenwich." He leaned closer to the map and found the Royal Observatory marked with a tiny dot right on the line. "The prime meridian," he read off the legend, and wrote the words down. London, then, was close to zero degrees longitude, and about fifty-one degrees north of the equator. He checked it twice, counting on his fingers along the printed lines.

"You know, my husband stood on that line at Greenwich," Mrs. Delgado said, smoothing the Thames poster until it hung straight. "Feet in two halves of the world at once. He said it felt like nothing, which somehow made it better." She held out a London brochure. "For your project. And tell your teacher we said come see us when your class picks a destination."

Oliver folded the brochure into his notebook, next to the numbers. Fifty-one degrees north, zero degrees longitude, a dot on a line drawn through a observatory by a conference an ocean away from it. He looked up at the crooked spot where the poster had been and saw it hanging level now, the river running bright across it.

"One foot on each side," he said. "Next time I'm in London, I'm doing that."

Mrs. Delgado laughed and pinned the brochure up in the window.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Havdalah, a Hebrew word meaning separation, is the ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night once three stars can be seen in the sky.
story:
Zoe had agreed to try her grandmother's Shabbat for one day, which meant no phone from Friday sundown until Saturday night. The hard part wasn't the food, since Grandma's challah was worth any number of missed snacks. The hard part was that her best friend Priya was sending updates about the school talent show tryouts, and Zoe had promised to follow every message. At sundown Zoe handed her phone to Grandma, who set it in the drawer under the translucent curtain of the front window, where the screen glowed faintly through the thin cloth like something underwater.

All Saturday Zoe found herself testing the rule. She decided that if rest was the principle behind the day, then watching Priya's messages could not count as work, so it should be allowed. She asked Grandma for the phone back with that argument. Grandma just said, "Try one full day, then tell me what you think," and went back to chopping apples. Zoe wrote her objection on a napkin and left it on the counter, which felt like losing an argument to nobody.

When the sky began to darken, Grandma's cousin Ruth, who was visiting, went to the front window and stood squinting upward. Zoe joined her. Ruth pointed at a pale dot above the neighbor's chimney, then a second one near the telephone wire. Zoe spotted the third herself, a faint point beside the chimney's shadow, and counted them out loud to be sure. "Three," she said. "Is three important?" Ruth nodded. "When we can see three stars, Shabbat is over. The ceremony after is called Havdalah." Zoe looked at the word Ruth had written on a scrap of paper and turned it over. On the back was a note in Priya's handwriting, folded and taped: "Tried out without you. Messed up the first line. You would have laughed. Telling you in person tomorrow." Priya had mailed it Friday, knowing the phone would be off.

Grandma opened the drawer and held out the phone. Zoe took it, then set it on the table instead. "The rest of the night is fine without it," she said. "Havdalah first." She carried the scrap of paper with the word on it to the window and looked for a fourth star.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players.
story:
Rain hammered the craft cabin, so Payton's cabin group dragged the camp's battered Monopoly box to the picnic table and set up between the glue buckets. By the time the storm had softened to a drizzle, Marcus owned half the board and Payton's shoe token was circling Illinois Avenue like a nervous herbivore avoiding a lion.

Then Maya landed on Marvin Gardens. She counted her money twice and pushed the deed back toward the bank. "I'm not buying it. It's too expensive and I need cash."

"Then nobody gets it," Marcus said, smug, and reached to move his token.

"Wait." Payton held up her hand. Something about this felt wrong, not because Maya was being stubborn but because the game seemed designed to handle this. "I think the rules actually cover it. Somebody grab the rule sheet."

Maya dug the folded paper out from under the board. They passed it around, three heads bent over the tiny print, until Payton's finger stopped on a sentence. "Here. If a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players."

Marcus groaned. "That's a real rule? Nobody plays that."

"That's the problem, though," Payton said. "You like it when we skip the rule, because then you keep your lead for free. So let's name it: the problem isn't Maya being broke. The problem is we've been inventing a house rule that helps whoever's already winning." She was careful to keep her voice level, even though her heart was going fast. "Fair fix: we follow the sheet for the rest of the game. Any auction, anyone can bid."

Maya grinned and knocked on the table like an auctioneer. "Marvin Gardens! Do I hear ten dollars? Going once."

Marcus sighed, dug into his stack, and raised four dollars. Payton raised six, mostly to simulate pressure, and Maya won it for nine. She slapped the deed down in front of her.

"Rent is twenty-five," Maya announced, "if you ever survive long enough to land there."

Marcus rolled the dice and muttered, "Thunder, take me now."

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users.
story:
Violet sat at her mother's desk on a Saturday, using the office computer because their laptop at home had died. She needed to find out why her science teacher had made the class debate one question all period: if a company pays to look like a normal search result, is that fair? On Monday each student had to bring one piece of evidence. Violet typed in "are ads fair" and got a page full of links about sneakers.

She tried again. "search results ads." Still mostly shopping pages. Her friend Dee had once told her that searching was like aiming a slingshot; sloppy words, sloppy hit. So Violet narrowed it. "search engine paid results rules." That worked. One link went to a government page, and she clicked it.

The page talked about the Federal Trade Commission. In 2013, the FTC had told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users. Violet read the sentence twice. Natural results, she realized, meant the ones the computer found on its own, and paid ones sat in the same list looking identical unless you caught the little label. She remembered a moment from Tuesday, a quick flashback that arrived whole: she had searched "best free math help," clicked the first blue link, and landed on a site that wanted her credit card for a "free trial." She had shut the page and blamed herself for not reading carefully. Maybe she hadn't been careless. Maybe the link had been dressed up to fool her.

Now she had a test. She opened a search page and typed "cheap headphones." The top three entries looked like ordinary results, but a small gray box in the corner of each one said "Ad." The fourth entry had no box at all. She tried "homework help," then "dog food," and counted each time. The boxes were small, but once she knew the rule, she could see the pattern everywhere, like suddenly noticing that the first three ducks in every flock wore collars.

She thought about her mother's lawyer talk, the way an amendment to a contract had to be spelled out so nobody was misled, and how a thick folder of papers could insulate a client from a bad deal only if every line was plain. Search results should work the same way, Violet decided, and the FTC seemed to agree with her mother.

Her mother came by with two granola bars and glanced at the screen. "Find your evidence?"

"Yep," Violet said. She highlighted the sentence and hit print. The printer started up with an abrupt clunk, and the page slid out warm into her hand.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Japanese uses different family words for your own family and someone else's: you call your own mother "haha" when talking to others, but a friend's mother is "okaasan."
story:
Jaxon stood in front of the Japan booth at the spring cultural festival, holding a paper card with his speech written on it. In ten minutes he had to introduce his family in Japanese, on the little stage under the luminous paper lanterns, and he still could not get through one sentence without messing it up. His partner for the booth, a girl named Mei who was hanging ceramic tea cups on a rack, kept glancing over at him.

"Ready?" she asked.

"Kore wa haha desu," Jaxon began, pointing at the photo of his mother taped to his poster. "Okaasan wa sensei desu. My mom is a teacher." Then he pointed at a drawing of his dog. "Inu wa..." He flipped his card over. "Inu wa totemo oishii desu."

Mei nearly dropped a cup. "Your dog is very delicious?"

"That's not what I wrote! I meant totemo isogashii, very busy. He's a busy dog." Jaxon laughed, but then his stomach tightened, because Mei was still looking at him strangely.

"You said okaasan," she said. "For your own mom, you say haha. Okaasan is for somebody else's mother, like mine."

Jaxon stared at his card. So that was why the girl in the practice video had switched words halfway through. He had thought she just messed up. There were two sets of family words, and he had been using them backwards. He grabbed a pencil, crossed out okaasan, and wrote haha above it. Then, to test it, he pointed at Mei and tried, "Anata no okaasan?"

"Hai," Mei said, grinning. "My okaasan is right over there, selling rice balls. She refuses to retire, so she works the festival every year."

When the booth announcer called his name, Jaxon walked to the stage. The lanterns glowed above him, and near the back an old fisherman was carving a wooden vessel, turning it slowly in his hands. Jaxon took a breath. "Kore wa haha desu. Haha wa sensei desu. Watashi no inu wa totemo isogashii desu." The audience clapped, and Mei gave him two thumbs up.

"Totemo oishii!" someone shouted from the back.

"Not delicious," Jaxon said into the microphone. "Busy."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Glossophobia is the name for fear of public speaking, and it is one of the most commonly reported fears.
story:
The speech was due on Friday, and by Wednesday Kaitlyn had written exactly one sentence. Ms. Reyes had drawn the shape of it on the board: a hook, three points, a closing, two minutes, no more. Kaitlyn's hook was "Has anyone here ever held a live octopus?" which was a lie, since nobody had, including her. She crumpled it up and started over.

The real problem was her hands. Every time she stood up in class, even to read a paragraph from social studies, her fingers buzzed like a phone on silent. In the bathroom before last period, she watched them shake in the mirror and made a decision: she would test whether the shaking had a pattern, like weather. If it only happened in front of the whole class, then the class itself was the cause, and something could be done about that.

She started small. At lunch she stood at the end of the table and gave her opening line to five friends. Her hands went quiet. Then Priya, who was next on the list for Friday, put down her sandwich and held out her own fingers, which were trembling over the tray. "It's called glossophobia," Priya said. "Fear of public speaking. My cousin told me it's one of the most commonly reported fears there is."

"You mean everybody's hands do this?" Kaitlyn said.

"Like a club," Priya said. "A huge, terrible club."

Kaitlyn felt the idea turn in her head, the way a rudder turns a slow boat. If half the room was secretly shaking, then shaking wasn't a personal failure; it was just the water everyone was sailing in. So on Friday she stood up, held her note card in both hands so the paper would hide the buzzing, and opened with the octopus question anyway. Nobody had held an octopus, and she said so, and the class laughed with her instead of at her. She sailed through her three points, closed with the octopus line turned upside down, and sat down as the timer beeped at exactly two minutes. Behind her, Priya walked to the front, gripped her note card, and began.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: A top, or apex, predator is at the end of its food chain and, as an adult, has no natural predators of its own.
story:
Mathis crouched between the tomato rows with his sketchbook balanced on his knees, trying to draw a food chain that started with the sun. His science teacher had said the chain had to run all the way to a top predator, and Ms. Okafor had promised the best poster would hang at the community garden's fall festival. Mathis wanted that spot on the fence more than he had wanted anything since the school talent show, where his magic act had flopped in a truly spectacular way.

He drew the sun with rays that radiate outward, then an arrow to the tomato leaves, then a fat green caterpillar chewing a leaf, then a songbird, and then, at the end, a hawk perched on a branch. His pencil hovered. Was a hawk really the end? Something about it bothered him.

That was when Priya from Plot 12 stomped over, dragging her watering can. "You put an owl at the top of my chain, and my cousin says owls get eaten by hawks, so hawks are the top, not owls."

"Not always," Mathis said. He flipped to a fresh page. "Let's test it. If the hawk is the last one, then nothing eats the hawk. Nothing." He drew a box after the hawk and left it empty. "My grandpa calls the last animal in a chain the apex predator. As an adult, nothing hunts it. It's at the end with no predators of its own."

Priya frowned at the empty box. "So an owl can be one too, if nothing eats the owl where it lives."

"Right. It depends on the chain." Mathis drew two chains side by side, hawk at the end of one, owl at the end of the other. Then he had another idea, and this one felt bigger. He crossed out the caterpillar in his first chain, hard enough to tear the page a little.

"Hey," Priya said. "Now your songbird has nothing."

"Exactly. Watch." He drew the songbird thin and hungry, then drew the hawk's box smaller, then put a big question mark after it. "You pull one link, and everything after it gets squeezed."

Priya grabbed her own pencil. "The garden fence. If we spray the caterpillars, the birds go, and then..." She trailed off, drawing arrows.

They worked until the sun dropped behind the apartments on Maple Street, the ones Mr. Ruiz was always worrying about losing to the bank because he couldn't pay his mortgage. Mathis taped both posters to the fence side by side and stepped back.

"Two top predators," Priya said, "one fence."

Ms. Okafor walked over with her thumbtacks already in her hand.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Overmixing muffin batter develops gluten in the flour, which makes muffins tough and can leave long tunnels inside them.
story:
Mathis turned the oven dial until the needle crept up to the number the recipe card demanded, three seventy-five, and then stood there feeling foolish, because preheating meant waiting with nothing to do. He wanted these blueberry muffins to be perfect. His sister Camille had laughed when he announced he would bake from start to finish with no help, and that laugh had been quietly thwarting him all morning, pushing him to make everything flawless.

He measured the flour, cracked the eggs, and folded the wet into the dry. The batter looked lumpy, though, speckled and uneven, and lumpy felt wrong. Last summer he remembered watching Grandpa whisk pancake batter until it poured like silk, and those pancakes had been the best he ever tasted. So Mathis kept stirring. He stirred until every lump surrendered and the batter gleamed smooth as frosting, then spooned it into the paper cups and slid the tray into the hot oven.

Twenty minutes later he pulled them out, golden and dome-topped, and broke one open while it still steamed. It was chewy in a way muffins should never be, and when he looked closer, long tunnels ran through the inside like wormholes. "What happened?" Camille asked, leaning over his shoulder. Mathis frowned at the crumb, turning the halves in the light.

"The recipe said stir just until combined," he said slowly. "I thought smooth was better. But the tunnels..." He'd read a warning on the back of the flour bag once, a line about gluten, and it surfaced now like a bubble. "Stirring too much makes gluten. Gluten makes them tough, and it leaves these tunnels." Camille raised an eyebrow, but he was already reaching for the bowl again.

There was enough batter left for six more. This time he counted his strokes and stopped while the batter still looked shaggy and lumpy, which felt naive but right. He scraped it into the cups, and while the second batch rose in the oven, he thought about how the first tray had taught him something no perfectly mixed bowl ever could. When the timer rang, he split a warm muffin open. No tunnels. Crumbly, tender, exactly what a muffin should be.

"Told you I'd do it," he said, and handed Camille the biggest one.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The phrase "according to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist.
story:
Grandpa dealt the cards and said, "We play according to Hoyle in this house." Payton's cousin Dex slapped his hand down on the table before anyone had even picked up their cards. "Last time we played Spoons, you grabbed my spoon," he said. "That's why I lost." Payton felt the old resentment rising, the kind that could ruin a whole dinner if she let it. She was about to shout back when she stopped and thought about Grandpa's word.

"Hoyle?" she asked instead. "Who's that? Some guy who makes up rules?" Grandpa smiled around a mouthful of potatoes. "Edmond Hoyle. His book from 1742 set down the rules of the card game whist. That's where the phrase comes from." Payton turned that over in her mind while Mom passed the green beans. So "according to Hoyle" just meant following the rules exactly, written down somewhere so nobody could argue about what they were. That was interesting, because right now she and Dex were about to argue about rules that had never been written down at all.

She laid her cards face down and looked at Dex. "Here's the problem. We've been playing Spoons two different ways, and neither of us ever said which way is the real one. You think grabbing is allowed if it's your spoon. I think you have to touch your own nose first." Dex frowned, but he didn't yell, which felt like a small miracle. "So whoever makes up the rule first wins forever," he said. "That's why I grabbed fast."

"No," Payton said. "Here's my idea. We test it. We write down one rule tonight, both agree on it, and we follow it exactly, like Hoyle. If it turns out bad, we change it before the next game, both of us together." She found a napkin and a pen from the junk drawer, and at the table, between the mashed potatoes and the rolls, they wrote: "You must touch your nose before taking a spoon." Dex read it twice, then nodded and shook her hand across the bread basket.

Grandpa cleared his throat. "You know," he said, "plenty of family fights have gone extinct the same way." Payton picked up her cards and grinned at Dex. "Deal me in. Nose first, spoon second."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: During puberty the larynx, or voice box, grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys.
story:
The waiting room smelled like mint and old magazines, and Landon was trying to read one upside down when his voice cracked right in the middle of a sentence.

"I'm twelve, not two," he had told his mom that morning, but now, telling the hygienist "I have a cavity on my left side," the word "side" came out in two pieces, a squeak and then a boom, like a door slamming on a mouse. His face went hot. At school last week his voice had cracked during his presentation on how bees pollinate apple trees, and he'd wondered about it ever since.

In the chair, he stared at the poster of a kid's growth chart, arrows pointing everywhere. Bigger feet. Broader shoulders. Then Dr. Kim leaned him back and said, "Say ahh," and Landon felt something in his throat he'd never noticed, a firm shelf that hummed when his voice went low.

"That's your larynx," Dr. Kim said. "Yours is growing, and so are your vocal cords, getting longer and thicker. That's why your voice is getting deeper."

Longer and thicker. Landon's brain lit up like the exam light above him. That was the pattern. His cousin Marcus was fifteen, and when Marcus talked it was like a tuba. Landon himself was more of a squeaky recorder. And the changes weren't just on the chart where you could see them. Some were hidden, like the sweat smell he'd noticed in gym class after his deodorant ran out and he'd kept using the empty stick for three days at the expense of his friendships, apparently, because Bruno had changed seats.

After the appointment, Landon marched to the pharmacy next door and bought deodorant with his own money, a significant purchase, two whole weeks of allowance. He also bought a little notebook. On the first page he wrote: VOICE, FEET, SMELL, ALL CHANGING. NOT A ROBOT GLITCH.

That night he pressed two fingers under Marcus's chin and made him talk, then did the same to himself in the mirror. The humming felt slower, lower, bigger.

"One day I'll sound like a tuba," he told his reflection. "A tuba that showers every day."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food such as milk should not sit out for more than two hours, or one hour above 32 degrees Celsius.
story:
Olivia counted the coins twice on the garage workbench, where Dad had set up a pretend store out of an old cardboard box. Three dollars and forty cents for the milk, so out of the five dollar bill Mom gave her, she should get one dollar and sixty cents back. She had to distinguish the quarters from the dimes by feel, because Dad kept turning the porch light off to make it harder. "Sixty cents, a dollar sixty," she said, and Dad slid the coins across the bench like a real cashier.

Mom's note was folded in Olivia's pocket, and she read it again at the end of the driveway. You can do this. Go straight to Mr. Patel's, buy one gallon of milk, come straight home. Love, Mom. It was the first time she'd ever gone alone, and the walk felt longer without anyone talking beside her. At the store Mr. Patel counted her change out loud, dollar sixty, and Olivia checked every coin before she put it in the bag with the cold gallon.

Halfway home, Zoe yelled from her porch. Olivia had been hoping for something spontaneous like this, an unexpected swim in Zoe's sprinkler, and she almost dropped the bag on Zoe's front step and ran. Then she stopped. It was over ninety degrees today, which meant over thirty-two Celsius, and last week she'd read a sign at the store that she hadn't been able to stop thinking about. Perishable food like milk should not sit out for more than two hours, and in heat above thirty-two Celsius, only one hour. She'd tested the rule in her head on the walk, counting the minutes, and now it mattered.

"We can't leave the milk out here," Olivia said. "It's way too hot. Can I put it in your fridge?" Zoe's mother said of course, and the girls carried it to the kitchen, then ran back outside and through the sprinkler until Olivia's shirt was soaked. When she finally walked in her own door, milk cold, change correct, Mom just looked at the clock and the receipt and then hugged her, wet shirt and all.

"Sixty seconds to spare," Olivia said, holding up the coins.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Telling an anxious friend to 'just calm down' rarely helps; listening without judging and taking their worry seriously usually helps more.
story:
Payton was measuring flour for Saturday's batch of snickerdoodles when her phone buzzed and buzzed and buzzed again. Maya was texting from her own kitchen two streets over, and the messages came fast: "I can't breathe right." "Tryouts Monday." "What if I freeze in front of everyone?" Payton set down the measuring cup, typed "just calm down, it's fine!!" and hit send, already looking forward to Maya saying thanks and then to the smell of cinnamon filling the kitchen.

The reply came back in three seconds: "WOW thanks. SO helpful. Nobody gets it." Payton stared at the screen. The flour dust on her fingers suddenly felt heavy. She had helped, hadn't she? She reread her own message and frowned. "Calm down" was what you said. It was what everybody said. Maya's next text arrived before she could think of anything better: "Forget it."

Payton paced between the counter and the stove, thinking hard. When her little brother cried about a nightmare, telling him to stop never worked either. What worked was sitting next to him and letting him tell the whole scary dream, start to finish. Maybe worry worked the same way. She tested the idea, typing slowly: "That came out wrong. Tell me what you're scared of. I'm listening for real." She added, "You don't have to make it short or summarize it. Send everything."

Maya sent eleven messages. Payton read every one, then answered each worry like it deserved a real reply: yes, freezing in front of the whole team would feel awful; yes, the new coach was intimidating; no, one bad tryout would not erase three years of practice. When Maya finally wrote "okay. that actually helped," Payton pumped her fist in the air and did a quick spin right there on the kitchen tile. She had been about to tell Maya that skipping tryouts seemed like the safe move, but she caught herself. That was her own bias talking, wanting to fix things fast. Listening had worked better, and listening was something she could do again anytime, no recipe required.

One text from Maya still glowed on the screen: "still scared tho." Payton thought about Mrs. Okafor, the counselor who kept a jar of fidget toys on her desk, and typed: "Tell Mrs. Okafor Monday morning. She's the right person for the big stuff. I'll walk with you." The oven timer dinged. Maya answered with a single word: "Deal." Payton slid the cookie sheet in and grinned at the warm orange light behind the glass.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: A passphrase of several random words, like the 2011 xkcd comic's example 'correct horse battery staple', is long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember.
story:
Brayden sat at the spare desk in his mom's office, staring at the setup screen for her new work laptop. "I can't reuse the one from home," Mom said, shaking her head. "If somebody guesses it there, they could get in here too. One password, everything gone." She handed him a sticky note with the office rules on it and went to her meeting. Brayden frowned at rule number four: create a strong password. His old one, dragon77, suddenly looked as flimsy as a paper towel.

He remembered last summer at his cousin Priya's house, when her account for a game had gotten broken into. "Somebody logged in from another country," she had said, "and they consumed all my gold buying dumb hats." Brayden had thought it was magic at the time. Now he wondered: how did a stranger even get her password? Probably because she used the same short one everywhere, so whoever stole it once could walk into everything else, like a key that opens every door on the street. That was the hidden pattern, invisible but real, and it made his stomach feel weird.

He scrolled through the company's tips page and found an old webcomic from 2011 taped to the bottom of the article, an xkcd comic, the caption said. In it, a stick figure compared a short jumbled password to a passphrase of several random words, and gave the example "correct horse battery staple." Brayden read it three times. Several random words were long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember? He glanced around the cubicles, half expecting a trap. "Correct horse battery staple," he whispered, and started to giggle. He could already picture it: a very precise horse standing next to a car battery and a staple. He would remember that forever.

But did it actually work? He decided to test it the only way he could think of. He opened the password checker tool the office provided, typed dragon77, and watched the bar flash red like a fire alarm. Then he typed seven-purple-burrito-tuba. Long enough to be hard to guess, easy for him to remember, and nothing like Mom's other passwords. The bar stretched green, elastic and satisfying, all the way across the screen. He did a small fist pump under the desk.

When Mom came back, he showed her the comic and the green bar, then his notebook page titled PASSWORD ANALYSIS, with three doodled horses. "Correct horse battery staple," she read, and burst out laughing. "That's ridiculous." "That's the point," Brayden said. "Ridiculous is memorable. Try making up your own." She chewed her lip, looked out the window at the parking garage, and started typing. "Wobbly raccoon elevator taco," she announced.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In a food chain diagram, the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.
story:
The trail smelled like wet leaves, and Rebecca had Mr. Okafor's folded poster jammed in her backpack like a crime she was trying to hide. Marisol's poster. Every arrow on it pointed the wrong way, so the grass appeared to be eating the rabbit, and the rabbit appeared to be eating the hawk, which Rebecca thought would be an interesting hawk but probably not a real one.

"Check this," she said, catching up to Marisol at the creek crossing. She flattened the poster on a boulder and jabbed a finger at the first arrow. "Which way is it supposed to point?"

"From the grass to the rabbit," Marisol said. "Obviously. Grass, then rabbit, then hawk."

"Right, but the arrow itself. Your arrow points from the rabbit to the grass." A dragonfly whirred past, and Rebecca watched it snatch something small out of the air. "I think the arrow goes the other way. From the thing that gets eaten to the thing that eats it. That's the direction the energy flows."

Marisol squinted. "So grass to rabbit to hawk."

"Grass gets its energy from the sun, the rabbit eats the grass, the hawk eats the rabbit. Each arrow shows the energy moving up the chain. Your version makes it look like every organism is being eaten by the plant." Rebecca flipped her pencil around and sketched it in the dirt, arrows small and neat. She was not a chronic poster-ruiner like Marisol, whose projects had suffered a long history of glue incidents, but even she could see this was fixable.

"Then erase and flip all eleven," Marisol said with a groan.

"You only have nine."

Marisol counted, twice, and got nine both times. Rebecca handed her the pencil and watched her flip each arrow, one by one, until the chain finally made sense. At the top, Marisol paused over the hawk.

"What if there's no hawk?" she asked.

Rebecca looked down the trail, where the grass grew thick and rabbits-shaped holes had been chewed into it. "Then a lot more rabbit."

Marisol drew a small arrow in the margin and wrote "sun" next to it. "Poor sun," she said. "Everything eats it and nobody says thanks."

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: Mayo Clinic advises against cleaning a cut with hydrogen peroxide or iodine, because both can irritate the wound.
story:
The paper cut came from a deposit slip, of all things, and it ran diagonally across Zachary's thumb like a tiny canyon. He had only come to the bank with his grandmother to set up his first savings account, and now he was bleeding on the counter while a teller named Ms. Ruiz unlocked a white box marked FIRST AID.

"Go on, fix yourself up," she said, sliding the kit toward him. "There's a bathroom mirror right over there."

Zachary carried the kit to the sink and flipped it open. Gauze, tape, little butterfly bandages, a brown bottle labeled iodine, and a fizzing familiar one: hydrogen peroxide. He reached for it automatically, because that was what his mom always grabbed, and the fizzing had always seemed like proof it was working. But taped to the inside of the lid was a folded first-aid guide from the Mayo Clinic, and one line stopped his hand midair. He read it twice. "Hydrogen peroxide and iodine can irritate the wound," it said, advising against both for cleaning a cut.

Huh. The fizzing wasn't cleaning, then? He wondered if the fizz was actually doing something harmful, or nothing at all. He decided to run a small test, since he couldn't see inside the cut anyway. He dabbed the peroxide on a scrape on his knee where he could watch the skin, then cleaned the thumb cut with plain running water and mild soap, the way the guide recommended. He pressed the edges together, laid a strip of tape across, and stuck a bandage on top, smoothing the ends down. The knee spot, an hour later in the car, looked redder than the skin around it, which made him think the guide had a point.

Back at the counter, his grandmother asked why he was grinning at his thumb. "I always thought the fizzy bottle was the strong one," he said. "Turns out the boring stuff works better." He was still thinking about hidden causes on the drive home, about how you couldn't see what was happening under a bandage any more than you could see the tapeworm in the parasite video from science class, quietly harming its host from inside. Some problems you had to judge by results. He decided he'd replicate his experiment on the next cut, just to be sure, and peeled back the bandage to peek.

"It's already knitting shut," he announced to the windshield. "Grandma, I'm basically a doctor."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Wet oven mitts can burn your hands, because water in the cloth carries heat quickly and can turn to steam.
story:
Connor had promised to bring something homemade to the school bake sale, and not just anything: the winners of the bake sale contest got their photo in the town paper, which everyone agreed was the most prestigious honor a sixth grader could earn without playing a sport. So on Saturday morning he stood at the counter with a recipe card, a bag of flour, and the feeling that he was about to find out whether he could actually do this alone. First instruction: preheat the oven to 375 degrees. He twisted the dial, watched the little orange light blink on, and wondered how the oven knew when it was hot enough. It had to have some kind of sensor inside, he decided, because the light didn't just click on and off at random.

He read the recipe twice before touching anything, the way his grandmother had told him to. Blueberry muffins: mix the dry, mix the wet, fold together without overbeating, fill the cups. When he got to the line that said "fold in blueberries," he paused. Fold wasn't a word he associated with baking. He tried it with a spatula, turning the batter over gently like he was tucking the berries into bed, and noticed how the streaks of purple slowly spiraled through the yellow. Maybe that was the point, he thought. Maybe stirring hard made the whole thing turn gray.

The batter went into the paper cups, the tray went toward the oven, and that was when his friend Maya walked in through the back door, home early from her sister's soccer game. "Smells good already and nothing's even baked," she said, hoisting herself onto a stool. "Also, is that a nut recipe? My allergy says I can only watch if there are no walnuts involved." Connor checked the card and showed her: blueberries only. Maya relaxed and stole a berry from the bowl.

When the timer finally buzzed, Connor grabbed the oven mitt from its hook beside the sink, where it had been hanging all morning. What he didn't know was that when he'd rinsed the berry bowl earlier, water had splashed up onto the counter and soaked one corner of that same mitt. He pulled it on, reached for the oven door, and Maya shot off the stool so fast it scraped the floor.

"Stop! It's wet!" She pointed at the dark patch on the cloth. "Water in the cloth carries heat fast, way faster than the dry part, and it can turn to steam. You could get burned right through the mitt." Connor stared at his hand, then at the oven door with its heat shimmering faintly above it. He tried to picture it: heat leaping through the damp weave while steam hissed up against his palm, all in the second it took to lift a tray. Slowly he peeled the mitt off, dried his hands and the counter with a dish towel, and swapped it for the dry one from the drawer.

The muffins came out golden, domed, and steaming gently in the morning light. Maya leaned over one, breathing in. "So," she said, "when we win that contest, do we split the credit sixty-forty, or do I get a whole muffin for saving your hand?" Connor laughed and slid the tray onto the wire rack. "You get first pick," he said.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United States, a bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president.
story:
Alyssa sat in the third row of the town hall with her notebook open on her knees. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, and someone had propped the side door open to let in the evening air. She had come for one reason: the newspaper had printed two different versions of a bill about a new bridge, and she wanted to know which one would become law.

She raised her hand during the question period. "The paper showed the House version and the Senate version, and the words aren't the same. Which one wins?"

A man in a green jacket stood up near the front. "Neither one wins yet. A bill has to pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president."

"Identical," Alyssa repeated, writing the word down. "So if they're different, nothing happens?"

"They have to agree on one exact text," the man said. "That's the rule."

Alyssa looked at her notes. In the House version, the bridge money went into a category called transportation. In the Senate version, it sat in a category called infrastructure. The sentences weren't just rearranged; they said different things. She raised her hand again.

"So the Senate can't just paraphrase the House bill and vote on that?"

"Correct," the man said, and a few people laughed.

After the meeting, Alyssa found her father by the coffee table under the luminous EXIT sign. She flipped her notebook to the page where she had copied both versions, then drew a box around the words that matched.

"They matched here and here," she said, tapping the page. "At first I thought the longer version was the real one. But it doesn't work like that. Nobody's version is real until both houses pass the same words."

"Which words do you think they'll pick?" her father asked.

Alyssa capped her pen. "I'm going to write to our senator and find out."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, such as carbon-12 with 6 neutrons and carbon-14 with 8.
story:
The kitchen table had disappeared under a lush carpet of blue and yellow pompoms, toothpicks, and a foam sphere with toothpicks already stuck in it like a strange cactus. Aurora counted out six yellow pompoms and pushed them into the sphere, then reached for the blue ones and stopped. Her science project was due at eight the next morning, and her friend Marisol was coming over in twenty minutes to finish the model together, which meant everything had to be decided before then.

Marisol arrived with her own bag of supplies and her own opinions. She dumped out a box of pompoms, held up a blue one, and frowned at Aurora's sphere. "You only put six neutrons in. I made mine at home with eight, because eight looked fuller. One of us has to redo it tonight."

"That's not fair," Aurora said. "I went first." But she didn't move to add the pompoms, because something was bothering her. Atoms of carbon had six protons; she knew that much, and she had counted her six yellow pompoms twice. If Marisol's sphere also had six protons, then both of them had carbon, even if the middle parts looked different. She turned the sphere slowly in her hands. "How many protons did you use?"

"Six, obviously," Marisol said. "It's carbon."

"So mine is carbon with six neutrons, and yours is carbon with eight neutrons." Aurora lined up two extra blue pompoms on the table beside her sphere, then picked them up and incorporated them into the foam, pressing them onto spare toothpicks. The middle of her atom grew rounder, heavier looking. "Same atom, different middle."

Marisol leaned over the model, her chin almost touching a toothpick. Then she sat back and delivered her verdict. "Then we build both. Yours with six, mine with eight, and we put them side by side on the poster."

"We can't call them the same thing on the poster, though," Aurora said. "People will think we messed up." She opened her science book and ran her finger down the pages until she found it, a short line under a diagram of two similar atoms. She read it twice, then looked up. "They're called isotopes. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons."

Marisol wrote the word on the poster in tall blue letters. "Carbon-12 for yours, carbon-14 for mine." They wired the electrons that night, nine small white beads circling each middle, and by eleven the poster was finished and drying flat on the table.

At school the next morning, their teacher paused in front of the poster and tapped the two models. "Nice work," she said. "Which one of you added the neutrons?" Aurora raised her hand and held up the extra blue pompoms still in her pocket. "We both did," she said.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Transition words such as first, however, furthermore and therefore link paragraphs and show the reader how one idea relates to the next.
story:
Emma's rough draft looked like five separate islands, and Mrs. Okafor had written one word in the margin: "Choppy." The essay was due tomorrow, and Emma wanted a B or better because the top three essays in the class would be read aloud at the school assembly. She sat at the corner table by the window, where afternoon light came through the tall glass and laid a long prism of color across the wood.

She read her paragraphs out loud in a whisper. "Dogs need exercise. Dogs help people relax. Dogs teach responsibility." Each sentence stood alone like a kid standing alone at a dance. Her friend Priya slid into the chair across from her with her own draft. "Mine got the same word," Priya said. "Choppy."

Emma stared at the prism on the table and turned her pencil over. She remembered a poster in the computer lab: a bridge between two cliffs. She flipped to the back of her binder, where she had copied phrases from a list on the board weeks ago. First. However. Furthermore. Therefore. "Transition words," she said slowly. "Maybe that's what the poster meant."

She tested it on her first paragraph. "Dogs need exercise. Furthermore, dogs help people relax." Then she tried the next pair. "However, some people think cats are easier." It was like watching stepping stones appear across a stream. Priya leaned over and read the new version. "It reads like one essay instead of five little ones," she said. "The words show how the ideas connect." Priya had said all morning that her own draft was hopeless and she would just turn it in as it was. Now she borrowed Emma's list and began adding words to her own sentences, crossing out, rewriting.

The two of them read the finished drafts aloud to each other in low voices. Emma's essay moved from her introduction, through her three reasons, and landed in a conclusion that began "Therefore, dogs make the best pets for families." The librarian glanced over and smiled at their whispers. Emma slid the draft into her folder and closed it. "Read yours again," Priya said. "The last part. Out loud this time."

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Anxiety triggers the body's fight-or-flight response, releasing adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and breathing even when there is no real danger.
story:
On the second day of Camp Pinewood, Scarlett noticed that her bunkmate Maya kept a hand pressed flat against her chest before every activity, even ones as small as the afternoon swim check. Maya wanted more than anything to read her poem at the Friday campfire, and she had practiced it to the birch trees behind the craft cabin until she could say it without the paper. But whenever Counselor Dana mentioned signing up, Maya went quiet, and her fingers did that thing against her chest.

At breakfast on Thursday, Scarlett counted. Maya's fork trembled, and she seemed to breathe in little sips, quick and shallow, though nothing dangerous was anywhere near the mess hall. Scarlett had a theory forming, something she'd heard her older cousin say once, and she wanted to test it. She grabbed Maya's wrist and found the pulse at the wrist bone. "Fifteen seconds," she said, watching the wall clock. "Sixteen beats. That's about sixty-four a minute, sitting still, eating pancakes." Maya blinked at her. "Why are you checking my pulse?"

"Because your heart is racing when nothing's happening," Scarlett said. "My cousin calls it fight-or-flight. Anxiety releases adrenaline, and adrenaline speeds up your heart and your breathing even when there's no real danger. Your body's acting like a bear walked in, but it's just pancakes." Maya laughed, a small cracked sound. "So I'm not broken?" "You're not broken. But you might need help with this, not just practice."

Maya had been ready to resign herself to skipping the campfire, watching from the log like always. Instead the two of them walked to Dana's table, and Maya, in a voice that shook only a little, said, "I want to read my poem, but my body freaks out. Can I sit near you while I do it?"

Dana smiled. "You can stand right beside me."

Friday night, Maya stood at the fire with her paper crushed in her fist, and Dana's hand on her shoulder, and she read the first line.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Frying an egg is a chemical change, because heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white so it turns solid and white.
story:
Hazel's science teacher had posted a challenge on the board: bring one mystery item from your kitchen, and the class would vote, physical change or chemical change. The winner got to dismantle the old toaster oven in the lab, taking it apart screw by screw, which was the only prize anyone cared about. Hazel wanted that toaster more than she'd wanted anything at school since October. But her item had to fool people, and she didn't have one yet.

On Sunday she slept over at Priya's house, and Priya's one wish was to cook breakfast entirely by herself, no help, because her older brother always claimed she couldn't. Priya cracked an egg into the pan and watched the clear white turn solid and white. "It's like a magic trick," she said, sliding it onto the plate. Hazel stared at it, fork paused in the air. When the egg cooled, she poked it, waiting for it to go clear again the way ice went back to water. It didn't. She nudged it. Still white, still solid.

"It won't go back," Hazel said slowly. "Ice melts back. This doesn't."

"So it's broken?" Priya said, worried her breakfast was ruined.

"No, it's..." Hazel turned it over with the fork. "It's like when Dad left the bike out in the rain and it rusted. That never un-rusted either."

In class on Monday, Hazel set the cold fried egg on the front table and said nothing. Kids voted physical change, six to four. Then she held up the phone video Priya had taken, the clear white going solid and white in the pan, and the shot of the cooled egg, unchanged. "Frying an egg is a chemical change," she said. "The heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white, so it turns solid and white, and it stays that way." The six voters groaned. Marcus, who had brought a squished marshmallow, muttered that stretching was obviously physical and this was rigged. The toaster oven sat on the back counter, and the teacher handed Hazel the screwdriver set.

Later, in the hall, Priya texted her brother a photo of the screwdriver in Hazel's hand with one line: "Told you I could cook."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero.
story:
Gabriella flopped onto the kitchen floor with the big atlas, the one with the coffee ring on Peru. With the recession tightening everything, Dad had said no trips this year, not even to Aunt Rosa's two states over. So Gabriella had made a deal with herself: if she could not go anywhere, she would learn to find every place on the map.

She already knew the trick for latitude and longitude, the crisscross of thin lines with numbers along the edges. You matched the horizontal number with the vertical one, and where they crossed, there was your city. Her problem was the opposite. She wanted to work backward, to name a city from its numbers alone, because Dad had promised a dollar for every capital she could locate without peeking at the labels.

She picked a hard one on purpose. The horizontal line, the latitude, read almost zero, and just a hair south of the equator line itself. She ran her finger along that line, past Africa, across the Atlantic, over the bumps of the Andes in South America. It was ironic, she thought, that a city sitting almost exactly on the equator, where the sun was straight overhead, should be famous for cool mountain air. Her finger stopped on a dot in Ecuador. She checked the edge numbers again, then persisted, sliding her fingertip sideways to the longitude line, tracing it down until both numbers crossed in one place. Quito. The capital of Ecuador.

She stood up so fast the atlas pages flapped. "Dad! Quito, Ecuador. It's less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero."

He came in drying a plate, looked at the atlas, looked at her, and pulled a crumpled dollar from his pocket. "Prove it."

Gabriella laid the ruler along the equator line and tapped the dot beside it. "See for yourself. Almost zero."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
